extraction.name: Are We on the Right Way for Evaluating Large Vision-Language Models?
extraction.description: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have recently achieved rapid progress, sparking numerous studies to evaluate their multi-modal capabilities. However, we dig into current evaluation works and identify two primary issues: 1) Visual content is unnecessary for many samples. The answers can be directly inferred from the questions and options, or the world knowledge embedded in LLMs. This phenomenon is prevalent across current benchmarks. For instance, GeminiPro achieves 42.9% on the MMMU benchmark without any visual input, and outperforms the random choice baseline across six benchmarks over 24% on average. 2)Unintentional data leakage exists in LLM and LVLM training. LLM and LVLM could still answer some visual-necessary questions without visual content, indicating the memorizing of these samples within large-scale training data. For example, Sphinx-X-MoE gets 43.6% on MMMU without accessing images, surpassing its LLM backbone with 17.9%. Both problems lead to misjudgments of actual multi-modal gains and potentially misguide the study of LVLM. To this end, we present MMStar , an elite vision-indispensable multi-modal benchmark comprising 1,500 samples meticulously selected by humans. MMStar benchmarks 6 core capabilities and 18 detailed axes, aiming to evaluate LVLMs’ multi-modal capacities with carefully balanced and purified samples. These samples are first roughly selected from current benchmarks with an automated pipeline, human review is then involved to ensure each curated sample exhibits visual dependency, minimal data leakage, and requires advanced multi-modal capabilities. Moreover, two metrics are developed to measure data leakage and actual performance gain in multi-modal training. We evaluate 16 leading LVLMs on MMStar to assess their multi-modal capabilities, and on 7 benchmarks with the proposed metrics to investigate their data leakage and actual multi-modal gain.

extraction.rai:dataCollection: MMStar is an elite vision-indispensable multi-modal benchmark comprising 1,500 samples meticulously selected by humans. These samples are first roughly selected from current benchmarks with an automated pipeline, human review is then involved to ensure each curated sample exhibits visual dependency, minimal data leakage, and requires advanced multi-modal capabilities. The process involves an automated pipeline to preliminarily filter out samples that do not meet visual dependency and LLM leakage criteria, followed by a strict manual review by three experts to ensure visual dependency, comprehensive capability assessment dimensions, and varying difficulty levels.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Samples are first roughly selected from current benchmarks, specifically two benchmarks focused on natural images and four centered on scientific and technical knowledge [27, 21, 51, 30, 20, 29].
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: An automated pipeline is used to preliminarily filter out samples that do not meet the visual dependency and minimal data leakage criteria. This involves using eight powerful LLMs (GPT4-Turbo, GeminiPro, LLaMA-70B, Qwen-1.5-72B, Mixtral-8x7B, InternLM2-20B, Yi-34B, Deepseek-67B) as candidates inspectors. Samples that could be answered by more than 2 of the 8 LLMs are excluded. The sample pool was reduced from 22,401 to 11,607 after this initial coarse filtering.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: After coarse filtering, three experts conduct a manual review process to ensure: 1) each sample’s answer is based on the understanding of visual content; 2) selected samples cover a comprehensive range of capability assessment dimensions; 3) most samples should require LVLMs to possess advanced multi-modal abilities for resolution. To expedite the manual selection of samples with varying difficulty levels for LVLMs, the hit counts of all 16 LVLMs on the coarsely filtered samples are tallied and split into four difficulty categories: easy (12-16), moderate (8-11), hard (4-7), and tough (0-3). Finally, 1,500 high-quality samples are manually curated.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: To expedite the manual selection of samples with varying difficulty levels for LVLMs, the hit counts of all 16 LVLMs on the coarsely filtered samples are tallied and split into four difficulty categories: easy (12-16), moderate (8-11), hard (4-7), and tough (0-3).
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Eight powerful LLMs (GPT4-Turbo [34], GeminiPro [41], LLaMA-70B [43], Qwen-1.5-72B [1], Mixtral-8x7B [19], InternLM2-20B [42], Yi-34B [49], Deepseek-67B [3]) were used as candidates inspectors for visual dependency and LLM leakage during the automated filtering pipeline.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: In the future, we plan to expand MMStar into a larger, online test set and explore dynamic evaluation methods to maintain sample visual dependency and reduce accidental data leakage into LLM’s and LVLM’s training corpora.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The MMStar benchmark is curated to mitigate biases found in existing benchmarks, specifically addressing issues where visual content is unnecessary for many samples and unintentional data leakage exists in LLM and LVLM training. The curation process aims for minimal data leakage and visual dependency.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Even the best model scores under 60% on average on MMStar, highlighting that the benchmark remains challenging for existing LVLMs. Future plans include expanding MMStar into a larger, online test set and exploring dynamic evaluation methods to maintain sample visual dependency and reduce accidental data leakage into LLM’s and LVLM’s training corpora, indicating ongoing challenges in maintaining benchmark integrity against evolving models.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: MMStar is designed to evaluate LVLMs’ multi-modal capacities with carefully balanced and purified samples. It is used for benchmarking 6 core capabilities and 18 detailed axes of LVLMs, assessing their actual multi-modal performance gains and data leakage degrees.
